findings:
Here's the case against `nullius wiring` fixing these three silences by just making them loud in place:

**It conflates three different failure modes under one banner.** A malformed JSON file, an unclosed frontmatter block, and "my resolver can't judge this" are not the same kind of gap. The first two are parse failures — the tool couldn't even read the input. The third is an epistemic limit — the tool read the input fine and chose not to rule. Bolting all three onto the same "report a line" mechanism means the report format has to simultaneously express "this file is broken" and "this reference might be fine, I just can't tell" — and those demand opposite user reactions (fix the file vs. shrug and move on). Collapsing them will either over-alarm on the ambiguous case or under-alarm on the truly broken one.

**"Loud" is not automatically the right fix for the ambiguous-resolver case.** That case is silence by *design* — the resolver declined because false positives are worse than a gap. Forcing it to emit a report line converts a deliberate abstention into a manufactured verdict category (UNVERIFIABLE-ish), and now the question is whether that new category itself needs anchors, fixtures, and a stable meaning — this is scope creep dressed as a bug fix.

**Fixing "silent" by adding output is the easy 80%; the hard 20% — deciding what severity each gets, and whether swallowed-parse-errors indicate a deeper problem with how the tool discovers config files at all — is being skipped.** Before writing code, this needs a design doc separating "can't parse" from "won't judge," not a single PR patching three call sites.
